abstract: We study the joint determination of tax evasion and charitable giving. A simple model in which individuals derive a warm glow from contributing to socially valuable activities predicts that congruence with the government determines whether tax payments substitute for private donations: under congruence, taxes and donations are warm-glow substitutes and donating-while-evading is dominated; under incongruence, donations retain their warm glow value while taxes do not, opening a region in the preference space in which evasion and donation are jointly optimal. We test the prediction using the seventh wave of the World Values Survey. Consistent with the theory, individuals with low levels of obedience and high prosocial motives are most likely to be observed in the donate-and-evade cell, and this concentration is stronger when individuals are not aligned with their national government---raising their odds of donating while evading by roughly one-quarter. Our results point to political congruence as a margin of tax compliance largely absent from the standard tax-compliance-and-morale literature, yet with implications for institutional design.
title: Paying Taxes Like Uli Hoeneß -- Tax Evasion, Charitable Giving, and Political Congruence

abstract: This paper provides novel evidence on the causal effects of juvenile incarceration on long-run labor market outcomes and family spillovers. We link criminal justice records from South Carolina to rich socioeconomic data and exploit quasi-random assignment of defendants to judges with varying incarceration propensities in an instrumental variables framework. Juvenile incarceration reduces earnings and employment during early adulthood for males. These earnings losses appear to operate primarily through reduced educational attainment, changes in mental health and behavior, and societal stigmatization, with adult incarceration having a modest role. For females, our analyses suggest that juvenile incarceration significantly increases earnings. These divergent gender effects can potentially be explained by a large reduction in teenage and early-adulthood fertility, which, in turn, may increase female labor market attachment. Finally, we document negative family spillover effects: connected children in the household experience lower educational attainment, suggesting that the broader social costs of juvenile incarceration may be larger than previously recognized.
title: The Social Costs of Juvenile Incarceration: Long-Run Effects and Family Spillovers

abstract: Strengthening the competitiveness of European regions is crucial to addressing global challenges and informing effective place-based policies. We examine how international linkages – specifically Global Value Chains (GVCs) – interact with Relatedness Density to shape the Economic Complexity of EU regions, conceived as a structural precondition for long-run competitiveness. Using a detailed region-sector dataset covering the period 2000-2010, the analysis shows that the effects of sectoral GVCs participation depend on existing capabilities. Less-complex regions are more likely to upgrade their Economic Complexity when GVCs participation is coupled with a more related local activity portfolio. This study provides fresh evidence on the interplay between global and local factors in promoting more balanced regional development across EU regions.
title: Complex to compete? The role of Global Value Chains and Relatedness Density in driving the Economic Complexity of EU regions

abstract: More connected networks are often regarded as more efficient, yet increased connectivity can elevate security risks, suggesting that sparser networks may be preferable from a security perspective. In this article, we study the trade-off between efficiency and security in networks. We develop a model in which a Defender and an Attacker engage in a two-stage game. First, the Defender builds a network by establishing costly links, where each node’s value is determined by its degree. Then, the Defender protects a limited number of nodes while the Attacker selects a node to target. Our analysis yields three main insights. First, by choosing the network’s degree sequence in the first stage, the Defender shapes the second-stage equilibrium and limits the expected loss from an attack. Second, the optimal network becomes sparser as link costs rise: a complete network is optimal when costs are low, while the centrally protected star, often regarded as the most secure configuration, arises only when costs are high. Third, when defensive resources are limited, a novel “maxi-core” structure arises in equilibrium, with a fully connected core surrounded by a sparse periphery.
title: Secure and Efficient Networks

abstract: Reaching net-zero CO2 emissions by 2050, as prescribed by the Paris Agreement, is hard to imagine without a carbon tax. This column estimates that reaching the goal by carbon taxation will require a tax path that peaks at around $1,300 per tonne of CO2, ten times current prices anywhere, and highlights how industries will bear very unequal transition costs. The intuitive smokestack principle, that the biggest direct emitters should pay the most, turns out to be false: costs are instead predicted by a simple statistic capturing how exposed an industry is through its supply chain.
